<!-- Rung M of climb batch 3 (explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.md, section M): a memo for
     TypeAnalyzer.parents and excludesClause, held on TraitTable behind a ProjectProperties switch.
     Written 2026-09-22 by the worker that made it. One line per paragraph. -->

# Rung M: the checker memo

problem: `explorations/perf-probes/nat/followup/f3-jfr-top.txt:40-44` (34,122 of 39,287 samples, 87%, have `TypeAnalyzerUtil.substitute` on the stack, `:40`; 33,892 of them, 86%, are under the lambdas of `TypeAnalyzer.parents`, 17,591 at shadow `:756`, `:41`, and `TypeAnalyzer.excludesClause`, 16,213 at shadow `:786`, `:42`, plus 88 at shadow `:783`, `:44`; those shadow lines are the tree's `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:726`, `:756` and `:753`, an offset of 30, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-analyzer-memo/probes/skeptic/citations.txt:37-40`), measured on the stock tree here as the checker-count stage taking 22.3-22.6 s with the memo off (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-analyzer-memo/probes/timing.txt:4-9`).
spec: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:207-215` (a trait type is a subtype of every type in its `extends` clause and excludes every type in its `excludes` clause), with `:163-164` (subtypes of excluding types exclude each other) and `Specification/basic/traits.tex:187-192` (the extension relation is the smallest relation the declarations induce): the two memoized functions compute these relations from the declarations and the type's arguments alone; the prose says nothing about how a checker computes them (`grep -rn -i -w 'memo\|memoize\|cache\|cached'` over `Specification/basic` and `basic-lib` finds only `basic/matrix-unpasting.tex:52-53`, on cache-oblivious matrix multiplication; `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-analyzer-memo/probes/spec-grep.txt`).
precedent: `explorations/perf-probes/nat/shadow.patch:656-715` (the prototype: one switch, `parents`/`excludesClause` routed through a memo, a global map keyed by `(traits, t)`), and the tree's memo shape `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:380-391` (`pExcMemo`: switch, `get`, compute, store), with one switch over two memos at `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:53`.
deviation: the memo is a pair of per-table maps on `TraitTable` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:81-97`), not a global map keyed by the table (`shadow.patch:710-715`), as the prototype's author asked (`explorations/perf-probes/nat/followup.md:96-98`); the switch `fortress.analyzer.clauses.cache` is read on the table beside the maps, not in `TypeAnalyzer.scala`'s block (`:63-69`), so that `TypeAnalyzer.scala` changes at its two call sites only (`TraitTable.scala:82`); the two bodies are wrapped by a by-name argument (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:722`, `:747`) instead of being split into a wrapper and an `Inner` function as the shadow and `pExc` do; the maps are `java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap` with `get`/`putIfAbsent`, not the `scala.collection.mutable.HashMap` of the tree's ten memos (`TraitTable.scala:83-84`, `:89-96`); no name visible to a Fortress program is added, so there is no specification spelling to differ from.
historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala`

## What landed

`TraitTable` gains a memo for each of `TypeAnalyzer.parents` and `TypeAnalyzer.excludesClause`, both behind one switch, `fortress.analyzer.clauses.cache` (default on): 20 lines added to `TraitTable.scala`: two imports (`:15`, `:26`) and the memo at `:81-97` with a blank line after it. In `TypeAnalyzer.scala` exactly two lines change, the two `def` lines: `parents` at `:722` and `excludesClause` at `:747` now pass their unchanged bodies to `traits.memoParents(t)` and `traits.memoExcludesClause(t)`. No line of `TypeAnalyzer.scala` is added or removed, so every line number in that file, rung P's `:443-457` and `pExcInner` included, is the same after this rung as at the batch base.

The count stage's table is identical line for line before and after (93 errors, 52 locations, the same `nat` crash, `#shadow` fresh), and so is the checker's full output behind it. The stage takes 9.5-12.4 s with the memo on against 22.3-22.6 s with it off (three alternating repetitions each, `probes/timing.txt`).

## What I inherited, and a setup step I took

Nothing: the worktree `/home/user/fortress-memo` and the branch `wip/rung-analyzer-memo` did not exist when this rung started (19:44 UTC; `git worktree list` showed the P, L and S worktrees only, and `git ls-remote` had no such branch). After a 40-second poll for it I created both with the recipe in `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md:103-109` — `git worktree add -b wip/rung-analyzer-memo /home/user/fortress-memo d610695c0c014001687e528fa9fd99078db6ea76`, `cp -a ProjectFortress/build` from the main tree, `mkdir tmp`, `git push -u origin wip/rung-analyzer-memo` — which writes the worktree's entry under the main tree's `.git/` and touches none of the main tree's files. The coordinator should know that the launch did not create this worktree.

Two operational notes. `ant compileAll` must run from the repository root; `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub that fails with "Premature end of file" (`ProjectFortress/build.xml:14-18`, "THIS FILE IS DEPRECATED"). And `ant compileAll` deletes the tracked `default_repository/caches/global.map`; the worktree restores it with `git checkout` before committing, and no commit of this rung carries it.

## Where this belongs

`parents` and `excludesClause` are `TypeAnalyzer` functions (`explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:95`, the `types/` package; `explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:188`, the trait-type row, whose checker column is `types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`). For a component, `StaticChecker` makes one `TraitTable` and one `TypeAnalyzer` over it (`map/modules-and-phases.md:357`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java:213-214`), and every further analyzer of that check is made from the first by `extend` or `extendJ` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:768-772`), which pass the same table on and start every per-instance memo empty. The checker makes new analyzers constantly: `scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:288`, `AbstractMethodChecker.scala:88` and `TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:57,66,76,85` each replace their analyzer with an extended one per generic declaration, and `STypeChecker.scala:189,202` extend per generic scope. So a memo on the analyzer would be dropped at every generic declaration; the table is the object whose lifetime is the whole check of one compilation unit, and it is what the two functions read. That is where the memo belongs, and where the prototype's author said it belongs (`explorations/perf-probes/nat/followup.md:96-98`).

The fix is not in a phase or in the library: the two functions answer the same question every time they are asked it, and nothing upstream can make them be asked less often without changing the checker's algorithms, which is not this rung's charter.

## Precedent search

**The tree already memoizes ten things in the checker, and none of them on the trait table.** `TypeAnalyzer.scala` has seven, each a per-instance `scala.collection.mutable.HashMap` behind its own switch in the block at `:63-69`: `pSubMemo` (`:97`, used `:113-121`), `pExcMemo` (`:380`, used `:384-391`) and the five normalize memos (`:504-508`, used `:523-611`). `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala` has two, `subtypeUAMemo` (`:90`) and `subtypeEDMemo` (`:148`), both behind the one switch `fortress.schema.subtype.cache` (`:53`, used `:95` and `:153`). `scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala` has one, `validOverloadingMemo` (`:441`, used `:453-458`), behind `fortress.analyzer.overload.cache` (`:77`). All ten have one access shape — switch, `get`, compute on a miss, store, return — and I copied that shape.

**A precedent with a defect, and the count.** The triage of 2026-09-22 found that `validOverloadingMemo` is keyed on a pair of declarations while its answer also depends on the other signatures and the oracle, and that it stores only `true`, so it hides 27-35 errors depending on build order (`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md:41`). That is the defect a memo can have: a key that omits an input. Of the ten, `validOverloadingMemo` is the one whose key visibly omits arguments of the function it memoizes (`signatures`, `isMethod` and `oa`, `OverloadingChecker.scala:443-448`, against the key at `:452`). The other nine key on the arguments of the function they memoize, or for the normalize memos on the parts of a type their authors chose (a variable's name, `:524`; a trait type's name and arguments, `:538`), and live on an owner whose remaining state is fixed for its life — the analyzer's `env` for `pSub`, `pExc` and the normalize memos, the schema analyzer's analyzer (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:52`) for the other two; I did not audit their bodies for a hidden input beyond that, which is outside this rung. So one of ten has the defect on its face, it is already on record, and this rung does not touch it. The memo added here reads nothing but its table and its key (next section), so it cannot have that defect.

**The prototype.** `explorations/perf-probes/nat/shadow.patch:656-715`: one switch (`probe.nat.noParentsMemo`, a system property), each function split into a wrapper and an `Inner`, the wrapper doing `getOrElseUpdate((traits, t), ...)` on a global `HashMap` in `object TypeAnalyzer`. Its author's own verdict: "a global `HashMap` in a companion object, keyed by the trait table, never evicted, not thread-safe; in the real edit it belongs on `TraitTable`, with the `ProjectProperties.getBoolean` switch the tree's other caches use" (`followup.md:96-98`). This rung does what that sentence says; the deviations are in the provenance block and argued under "The decisions".

## Why the memo changes no answer

**What the two functions read.** `parents(t)` reads `typeCons(n)` for the trait's name, that index's `extendsTypes` and `staticParameters`, and `t`'s arguments, and returns their substitution (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:722-727`). `excludesClause(t)` reads the same index's `excludesTypes`, `extendsTypes` and `staticParameters`, substitutes, and recurses on each substituted supertrait (`:747-762`). `typeCons` is the table's `typeCons` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:708-710`, `TraitTable.scala:33-74`), and `substitute` is a pure function of its three arguments (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzerUtil.scala:35-60`: a map from parameter names to arguments and a tree walk). Neither function reads the analyzer's `env` or any of the analyzer's memos. So both are functions of the table and the type, which is the whole of the memo's key and owner.

**The table does not change.** `TraitTable` has no mutator: its two constructor parameters, `current` and `globalEnv`, are never reassigned (`TraitTable.scala:32`), and the memo is created with the table and dies with it. What the table reads beneath it does not change during the table's life either: a `CompilationUnitIndex` wraps its type constructors in `CollectUtil.immutable` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/index/CompilationUnitIndex.java:41`); the only mutators of a trait's clauses, `ProperTraitIndex.addExcludesType` and `addComprisesType` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/index/ProperTraitIndex.java:43-49`), are called from `IndexBuilder.checkTraitClauses` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/IndexBuilder.scala:235,245,261`), which runs while the index is being built (`:175`), and from the unit-test helper `TypeParser` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/TypeParser.scala:131-132`), which does so before it makes its table (`:173`); `extendsTypes` and `staticParameters` have no setter (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/index/TraitIndex.java:60,77`). Every place the checker, the desugarer or code generation "changes the trait table" in fact constructs a new one, with empty memos: the eight construction sites are `StaticChecker.java:213`, `Desugarer.java:121`, `CodeGenerationPhase.java:81,179`, `scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:73`, `scala_src/overloading/OverloadingChecker.scala:52`, `AbstractMethodChecker.scala:58` and `TypeParser.scala:173`, and `TraitTable` has no subclass. A table can outlive a rebuilt index — `StaticChecker` rebuilds the component index after type checking (`StaticChecker.java:248`) and keeps using the analyzer over the old table for the second well-formedness check (`:268`) — but that is the tree's behaviour with or without the memo: the table reads the index it was built over either way, and the memo returns what that table would compute.

**What a hit can return that a recomputation would not.** Keys are compared by `equals`, and the AST's `equals` ignores source spans: `SpanInfo.equals` is true for any two (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/SpanInfo.java:46-55`), and `TypeInfo.equals` compares only static parameters and where clause (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/TypeInfo.java:58-73`). So a hit for a type equal to an earlier key returns the earlier call's result, whose substituted arguments carry the earlier call's spans and the earlier call's parenthesized flags: `TypeInfo.equals` and `TypeInfo.generateHashCode` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/TypeInfo.java:58-72`, `:81-87`) leave out the `_parenthesized` field `TypeInfo` inherits from `ParenthesizedInfo` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/ParenthesizedInfo.java:24`), just as they leave out the span (the second skeptic's correction). Nothing else can differ: `TraitType.equals` covers the name, the arguments and the trait's static parameters (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/TraitType.java:74-95`), which is all `typeCons` and `substitute` read. The tree's normalize memos already have this property (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:537-545` stores a normalized trait type under its name and arguments). I looked for both where they could show — located error messages, the serialized checked ASTs, which carry spans and the flag, and the class files — and neither shows: see the differentials below.

**Recursion.** `excludesClause` calls itself from inside its own computation, so the memo cannot use `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent`, whose mapping function must not modify the map (the JDK documents this, and detects some cases with `IllegalStateException: Recursive update`); `memo` does `get`, computes outside the map, then `putIfAbsent` (`TraitTable.scala:89-96`), the same order as the tree's ten memos. A cyclic hierarchy recursed without end before the memo and still does; the memo stores nothing until a computation returns, and an exception (`typeCons`'s "Not in the trait table", a `ClassCastException` on a non-trait index) stores nothing either.

**Threads, the column the batch record names.** The checker runs on one thread: the JFR recording's 39,287 samples were "all on thread \"main\"" (`explorations/perf-probes/nat/followup/f3-jfr-top.txt:8`), and there is no thread, executor or fork-join use in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/`, `scala_src/` or `repository/` (the one `ForkJoin` hit, `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:651`, is a descriptor emitted into generated code). The four-thread gate runs execute compiled programs, and no file under `runtimeSystem/` names `TraitTable` or `TypeAnalyzer` (the 37 files that do are all compiler-side: under `compiler/`, `scala_src/` and `repository/ForeignJava.java`). So no two threads can reach one table in today's tree. The maps are `ConcurrentHashMap`s all the same: values are immutable Scala sets computed from immutable inputs, so two threads that race on one key compute equal values, one `putIfAbsent` wins, and `memo` returns the stored one (`TraitTable.scala:93-94`).

## The test, and what it recorded

The rung declares `testIsStage`: there is no `.fss` program that can go red for a cache. The stage is `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`.

**Recorded before the edit** (after `ant compileAll` on the batch base, nothing edited): `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-analyzer-memo/probes/checker-count-preedit.txt`, committed in `3264d93e6` before the edit commit `fe83db93e`. Key line: `#total	93`. It is byte-identical to the gate's comparand `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/checker-count.txt` (`diff` empty).

**Recorded after the edit** (after `ant compileAll` with the edit, switch at its default): `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-analyzer-memo/probes/checker-count-postedit.txt`. Key line: `#total	93`.

# Rung P (rung-exclusion-relax): the record lines to fold at merge time

Taken into the tree at the gather of climb batch 3 (2026-09-22) as the record of a rung that did not land: its source stays on `wip/rung-exclusion-relax`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExclusionRelaxRungP.fss` and `.test` included, which the text below cites as in the tree, and the provisional ledger row 354 and row-97 note it proposes were not opened (ledger row 354 is rung L's); see `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-3/RECORD.md`, "Not landed". Every file under `probes/` that the text cites is in the tree: two taken at the gather, the other sixteen byte-identical from the branch at the batch's merged-diff review.

The rung stopped. It lands no checker change. Its net change outside `explorations/` is one expected-failure test, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExclusionRelaxRungP.fss` and `.test`, which is green on the base checker. The full account is `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/REPORT.md`.

## FACTS.md

- **The compiled checker's `checkP` is the Fortress designers' own rule, "multiple instantiation exclusion", not an accident.** Sources: the OOPSLA 2011 paper, `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152` ("Fortress imposes a rule that forbids multiple instantiation inheritance ... We call this rule multiple instantiation exclusion and adopt it here"), and Karl Naden's writeup of 2012-08-31, `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:476-478`, `:496-497` ("specialization of generic functions or multiple instantiation inheritance, but not both"; "Ultimately, Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion"). The rule is enforced by `TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:178`, `:187`, and the Return Type Rule check relies on it (`scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`). The interpreter took the other side of the trade-off: no instantiation clause in `FType.java:197-297`, and generic overloads without an excluding pair are refused (`OverloadedFunction.java:496-498`). The specification sides with the interpreter on both halves (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:184-189`; `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`). The compiler prelude's commented-out `extends` clauses (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:1483`, `:1521`) are the compiled world keeping within the rule. (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/REPORT.md`, "The stop")
- **Relaxing `checkP` alone is unsound on the compiled path, in every placement** (the two hierarchy questions; those plus the overloading check; every analyzer). `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/ProbeMIEPick.fss` (`BadList` in six lines) type-checks under all three and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`: a `Tag[\String\]` variable holds an object that is only a `Tag[\ZZ32\]` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/probe-matrix.txt:67`, `:89`, `:111`). On the rung's own branch the checker count is 33 under each placement and 93 unrelaxed (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-off.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-hier.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-over.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-broad.txt`). The overloading half also refuses a compiled program that works today, overloads on `Tag[\ZZ32\]` and `Tag[\String\]` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/probe-overload.txt`). Rung P of climb batch 3 stopped on this, 2026-09-22.

## Ledger

**New row 354 (provisional; the gather assigns the final number in manifest order P, L, C, R, S, M).** Suggested cells, in the ledger's column order (`| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:57`):

- claim: **multiple instantiation, the two paths on opposite sides of one trade-off.** The compiled checker refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic (`checkP`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-456`; `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExclusionRelaxRungP.fss`, 4 errors). It accepts a generic function specialised for one instantiation (`pick[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `pick(t: Tag[\ZZ32\])`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/ProbeMIEPickCtl.fss`, compiles and runs). The interpreter does the reverse: `FType.java:197-297` has no instantiation clause, and `OverloadedFunction.java:496-498` refuses the specialised overload (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/walk-ProbeMIEPickCtl.txt:5-6`). Relaxing `checkP` without also refusing the specialised overloads is unsound: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/ProbeMIEPick.fss` links and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` under the hierarchy-only, hierarchy-plus-overloading and broad placements (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/probe-matrix.txt:67`, `:89`, `:111`).
- status: NEGATIVE-VERIFIED
- class: design decision (the two implementations disagree, and the compiled one follows the designers' 2011–2012 papers against the 2008 specification)
- spec citation: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:184-189` (exclusion is the smallest relation, with no instantiation clause) and `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105` (differing static parameters are an error); against both, the designers' rule, `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152` and `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:476-478`, `:496-497`
- reproducer: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/REPORT.md`; `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/probe-matrix.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/probe-overload.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/walk-ProbeMIEPick.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/walk-ProbeMIEPickCtl.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/walk-ProbeTypecaseMIE.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-off.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-hier.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-over.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/checker-count-broad.txt`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/xxx-tripwire.txt`
- found by: rung P, climb batch 3, 2026-09-22
- notes / workaround: a decision, not a patch. Either keep the rule on the compiled path, and then the interpreter library's nested tower cannot be checked as it stands. Or relax `checkP` in the positive direction together with enforcing `overloading.tex:100-105` in `scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala`, which is decision (b) of `explorations/perf-probes/nat/triage.md:52-59`, `:113`. The placement of the relaxation then also has to cover the `typecase` redundancy checks (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:268`, `:274`, `:280`, `:332`) and the meets of `normConjunct` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:632-640`); `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/ProbeTypecaseMIE.fss` shows that only the broad placement reaches them. Gated: `XXXExclusionRelaxRungP` goes red when `checkP` is relaxed for the hierarchy (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/xxx-tripwire.txt:23-43`).

**Note to append to row 97** (rows are never renumbered or moved): "2026-09-22, climb batch 3 rung P: the compiled path accepts this shape and dispatches it correctly, because its checker implements multiple instantiation exclusion (`checkP`), so two instantiations of one generic exclude and the pair needs no meet. Measured on `f(t: Tag[\ZZ32\])` beside `f(t: Tag[\String\])`: compiled, runs; `walk`, refused as this row says (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/probe-overload.txt`). Relaxing `checkP` for the overloading check makes the compiled path refuse it too. See row 354 (provisional)."

## Handover state line

Rung P (the exclusion relaxation) **stopped** and lands no checker change. The clause is the designers' "multiple instantiation exclusion" (OOPSLA 2011; Naden 2012), which the Return Type Rule check relies on. Relaxing it alone lets a six-line `BadList` program type-check and die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` under every placement, so the batch's 23 is not reachable without a decision from Pavol. The choice: keep the rule on the compiled path (then the library's nested tower cannot be checked as it stands), or drop it together with enforcing `overloading.tex:100-105`, which is triage decision (b). Landed from P: `compiler_tests/XXXExclusionRelaxRungP` (expected failure, green) and the record under `compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/`. The count on P's branch is 33 under each placement, 93 as landed. The merged tree's count is L's 102 if L lands alone.

## For the coordinator

- **Manifest consequence.** With P stopped, the gate's count after the batch is L's declared 102, if L lands, not 23. L's declaration already covers "P refused and L lands alone" (`CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:67`).
- **Gather.** The worktree and the branch were created by this rung itself, because neither existed at launch (REPORT, "Inherited state"). `ProjectFortress/build` in the worktree holds the measurement build (base plus `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/probes/measurement-switch.patch`); with `-Dprobe.rungP` unset it behaves as the base checker.
- **The question for Pavol**, in one line: on the compiled path, keep multiple instantiation exclusion (the designers' choice, and the interpreter library's tower must then change), or drop it together with the static-parameter sentence (the specification's choice, and specialised generic overloads such as `pick[\X\]` beside `pick` become errors)?

The rung cannot land the relaxation alone, the closure it needs is the decision the batch record itself reserved to Pavol (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:18`, "35 the specification's sentence on differing static parameters, which is Pavol's decision"; `explorations/perf-probes/nat/triage.md:113`), and the record's own stop clause for this rung names the case (`CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:85`, "the fix for that is a second design decision"). What reaches Pavol is narrower than the worker's two-way choice, and section 6 states it with costs measured in this ruling.
     6	
     7	Nothing was built or run for this ruling. It rests on the branch's net change (`git diff d610695c0...9066c6d18`: two files under `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`, the rest under `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/`; nothing under `ProjectFortress/src`), the worker's REPORT.md and record.md, the probes and captures on the branch, the specification passages read with their surroundings, and the precedents at the cited lines.
     8	
     9	## 1. What the specification settles, and how
    10	
    11	The specification is not silent. It speaks on both halves of the problem, and its two halves form one coherent design.
    12	
    13	**(H) A type may extend two instantiations of one generic.** `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:184-189`: the subtype and exclusion relations "are the smallest ones that satisfy all the properties given in those sections (and this one)", and the properties that make trait types exclude are an `excludes` clause (`:212-214`), arrow, tuple, `()` and `BottomType` (`:215-216`), object-ness (`:222-224`) and propagation to subtypes (`:163-164`). None concerns two instantiations. The worker cited this and it is right. The worker cited `trait-parameters.tex:339-351` as text and conceded it is the covariant case that Naden's refinement permits (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:536-537`). It missed the two passages that are decisive and invariant:
    14	
    15	- `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:359-367`: `trait C extends D[\T\] where {T extends Object}` — "In this declaration, trait C is a subtrait of *every* instantiation of parametric trait D. Thus, trait C has all of the methods of every instantiation of D." Under multiple instantiation exclusion, "any type which is a subtype of two distinct instantiations of a single generic type is equivalent to Bottom" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:345-347`), so `C` would be uninhabited; the specification instead discusses the inference restrictions `C` needs (`:367-379`), which only a live type needs.
    16	- `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:383-397`: `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}` — a single value that is a member of every instantiation of `List`. This is `BadList` (`justificationOfRTR.tex:89-98`) written on purpose, as the specification's canonical empty list. Note that its `first()` and `rest()` throw (`:392-393`): the specification's own example never produces a `T`, which is why it is sound in the specification's world.
    17	
    18	So on (H) the specification settles it against the compiled checker's `checkP` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-456`) and against the two hierarchy questions that enforce it (`scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:178`, `:187`). The worker's four errors on the MinP shape (`probes/test-preedit.txt:2-10`) are that enforcement.
    19	
    20	**(O) Overloaded declarations share their static parameters, and a call site instantiates them once.** `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-108`: "it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to α-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them. Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable". With `trait-parameters.tex:374-379` ("It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site ... type checking rejects the program" otherwise), this is the specification's dispatch model: static arguments are fixed at the call site by inference, every overload of the name is instantiated at those arguments, and dispatch chooses among declarations that all carry the same instantiation. In that model `Empty` is harmless: no overload of a name can be applicable to it at an instantiation other than the caller's, because no overload has an instantiation of its own.
    21	
    22	**The two worlds.** The specification's world: (H) allowed, (O) enforced, call-site instantiation; no need for multiple instantiation exclusion. The 2011–2012 design's world: specialised generic overloads wanted (`tail[\X\]` beside `tail`, `justificationOfRTR.tex:76-84`), which (O) forbids outright; run-time instantiation for dispatch (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation`, the title itself); and multiple instantiation exclusion adopted to make that sound (`Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`; `justificationOfRTR.tex:457-459`, `:476-478`, `:496-497`). Each world is coherent. The compiled checker implements the second (the worker showed this, correctly). The interpreter is on the specification's side of (H) (`interpreter/evaluator/types/FType.java:197-297`, no instantiation clause) and has its own rule on the overload side (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:496-498`). Rung P as briefed — the interpreter's (H) with the compiler's run-time-instantiated specialised overloads — is the one combination that belongs to neither world, and the worker's `probes/ProbeMIEPick.fss` is the program that shows it: links under every placement and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`probes/probe-matrix.txt:64-68`, `:86-90`, `:108-112`). That measurement is right and it is the load-bearing fact of this rung.
    23	
    24	## 2. Where the worker was right
    25	
    26	- `checkP` is the designers' "multiple instantiation exclusion", by name and by rationale: `exclusion.tick:141-152` (read at `:125-165`); `justificationOfRTR.tex:76-98`, `:342-347`, `:457-459`, `:476-478`, `:496-497` (read with their surroundings). The batch record, the trace and the triage do not cite either source; the record's "designers' survey" is `explorations/run-c4/cold-cache/operators/D/SURVEY.md:46`, a revival-era note about the interpreter. All correct.
    27	- The Return Type Rule check solves for one instantiation of the less specific declaration and trusts it: `scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`, `subEDsolution` at `:88`, the substituted return type at `:95`. Correct, and it is exactly the reliance Naden's proof names (`:449-459`).
    28	- Relaxing `checkP` alone is unsound under every placement, and the control without the multiply-instantiated type runs correctly everywhere (`probe-matrix.txt:18-21`, `:60-63`, `:82-85`, `:104-107`). Correct; the captures were read.

Correct.
    30	- The overloading half of the record's placement refuses row 97's shape, which the compiled path accepts and runs today (`probes/probe-overload.txt:2-6` against `:12-19`, `:24-31`). Correct, and this cost was not in the record.
    31	- The compiler prelude's commented-out `extends` clauses (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:1483`, `:1521`) are the compiled world staying inside the rule. A sound reading of lines the trace could not explain (`explorations/perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md:167-180`).
    32	- The expected-failure test `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXExclusionRelaxRungP.fss` and `.test` is the right home-2 artifact for (H): it asserts the specification's program, fails today, and was shown red on the deliberate local fix (`probes/xxx-tripwire.txt:17-21`, `:26-43`, `:48-61`). The mechanism is `FileTests.java:384-404` (the `shouldFail` branch of `SourceFileTest`: a failure with `link_err_contains` satisfied is "Saw expected failure"; a successful link leaves `link_err_contains` unsatisfied, so `trueFailure` is set and the test is red as "Saw wrong failure"). It stays on the branch; whichever rung lands the relaxation converts it to the positive test the record asked for.
    33	
    34	## 3. Where the worker was wrong or incomplete
    35	
    36	1. **"Keep multiple instantiation exclusion on the compiled path" is not a live candidate**, and the worker presented it as one of Pavol's two choices (REPORT.md, "The stop", option 1; record.md, "The question for Pavol"). It is refused by the specification at `trait-parameters.tex:359-367` and `:383-397` (section 1), not only by the "smallest relation" sentence; and it is refused by the decided library route, `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:45` (one library, the interpreter's; "How the checker is brought to accept the library — the exclusion sites, ... — is a plan put to him step by step, not a decision to re-ask"). Keeping the rule means the checker can never accept the library's nested tower (61 errors at 26 sites, `CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:73`), so it is the library route re-asked. The designers adopted the rule to buy specialised generic overloads that the specification forbids (`justificationOfRTR.tex:76-84` against `overloading.tex:100-105`); the revival is not bound to buy them.
    37	
    38	2. **"Drop it together with enforcing `overloading.tex:100-105`" over-states what soundness needs.** The hole is the Return Type Rule check trusting one instantiation (`OverloadingOracle.scala:88-95`). The sentence closes it, but the sentence is a restriction on every overload set, generic-beside-generic included, and its cost was left unmeasured by the worker (REPORT.md, "What this does not settle", third item). Measured here by a column-0 grep for a declaration `name[\...\](` beside `name(` in the same file (functional methods and nested declarations not counted, so a lower bound): `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/Compiled12.invariantInference.fss:52-61` (run by its `.test`) and `compiler_tests/Compiled6.ak.fss:14-15` (a bare `.fss`; whether the suite runs it was not checked); `library_tests/` 0; `LibraryBuiltin/` 0, so the compiler prelude has none; the interpreter's library `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57` (`takeleft[\T\](a: Nothing[\T\], b: Any)` beside `takeleft(a: Any, b: Any)`, and `takeright` the same); and in the interpreter's gated `tests/`, `overloadTest8.fss:33-37`, `doubledOverloading.fss:36-41`, `GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, `ArrayListQuick.fss:36-55` and `PureListQuick.fss`. Every one of these return types is `String`, `()`, `ZZ32` or the parameter-free `Any`: none mentions the generic's parameter, so none has the hole, and the sentence would refuse all of them for no soundness. This is the measured cost that makes the sentence Pavol's and not a repair worker's.
    39	
    40	3. **The interpreter's rule is narrower than the worker reads it.** `OverloadedFunction.java:496-498` refuses a pair when a symbolic type was seen or a parameter pair is *unrelated* and nothing excludes; `walk` accepts `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57` and `tests/GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, both one-generic-one-not, both subtype-related in every position. The worker's table cell "interpreter: refused" is measured for the `Tag[\X\]` beside `Tag[\ZZ32\]` shape (`probes/walk-ProbeMIEPickCtl.txt:5-6`) and must not be generalised to every specialised overload. The error text itself says what the test is: "unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present" (`probes/probe-overload.txt:39`).
    41	
    42	4. **Home 3 for `pick[\X\]` beside `pick` is the right home for the wrong reason.** The worker gave it home 3 so as not to pre-empt decision (b) (REPORT.md, "The three homes", item 2). An XXX file is deleted with the decision either way, as the worker itself says of the other XXX file, so that reason does not hold. The reason that holds is mechanical: a program that links and runs today cannot be an expected-failure test. In `FileTests.java:384-404`, an XXX test whose link succeeds and whose run exits 0 has `anyFails` false and `trueFailure` null, and is red today as "Missing expected failure" (`:399-402`); with `link_err_contains` set it is red as "Saw wrong failure" (`:394-397`). Home 2 has no working form for "accepted today, the specification says refuse", so the probe and the ledger row are the only home. The record should say this, not the pre-emption argument.
    43	
    44	5. **The trade-off is not symmetric in the way the worker's table suggests.** The worker's table says "either column's pair is sound". The specification's column is sound because of the call-site instantiation model (`overloading.tex:106-108`, `trait-parameters.tex:374-379`), not because of (O) alone; the 2011 column is sound because of multiple instantiation exclusion. Whether the compiled code generator instantiates a dispatched generic overload from the call site's static arguments or by inspecting the argument's run-time type is the fact on which every sound closure short of the full sentence depends (Naden's `headOrID`, `justificationOfRTR.tex:481-494`: without the rule "we need to choose an instantiation without any means to do so"). The worker did not name this, and neither the trace nor the triage measured it. `ProbeMIEPick` shows only that a *non-generic* specialisation is chosen at run time regardless of the call site's `X = String`.
    45	
    46	## 4. Why this is a reserved fork and not a silent specification
    47	
    48	Rule 4 of the brief: the specification answers a divergence; a silent specification is the reason to think harder, not to stop. The specification here is not silent. On the divergence "`pick[\X\]` beside `pick`: compiled accepts, `walk` refuses" it sides with `walk` (`overloading.tex:100-105`), which is rule 4's first outcome, repair. The repair is the sentence, and the sentence is what the batch record reserved to Pavol before this rung ran (`CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:18`; `triage.md:113`, "(b) is Pavol's decision about the specification, not a patch: the 35, and the sentence's reach over overrides"). It was reserved because the library the route makes the standard uses shapes the sentence refuses (the triage's 35 sites; `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57` in this ruling), and `POSITIONS.md:39` makes the library's practice the standard. A judge does not lift a reservation the coordinator wrote into the record Pavol launched with "go".
    49	
    50	The candidates short of the sentence were derived and each falls on a stop of its own:
    51	
    52	- The interpreter's rule ported to the compiled checker (a symbolic pair needs an excluding or subtype-related position everywhere) refuses generic-beside-generic sets with overlapping unrelated domains that the sentence permits (same parameters, different domains), which is a change of semantics against what the specification does say — `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:52`'s fork.

    55	
    56	So every sound closure is the reserved sentence, or against the specification in a corner, or conditional on a fact about the code generator that no one has measured. That is the second design decision `CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:85` names, found by a probe instead of by the suite. Stop.
    57	
    58	## 5. Rulings on the branch as it stands
    59	
    60	- The XXX test stays. It is the home-2 tripwire for (H), shown red on the local fix. No positive test lands, because no relaxation lands.
    61	- The record's FACTS line on the rule's provenance stands, with the two citations of section 1 added (`trait-parameters.tex:359-367`, `:383-397`).
    62	- The record's FACTS line "relaxing `checkP` alone is unsound in every placement" stands as measured.
    63	- The provisional ledger row (354 in the worker's numbering; the gather assigns the number) stands, with its "notes / workaround" cell corrected: strike "keep the rule on the compiled path" as a candidate, and replace "or drop it together with enforcing `overloading.tex:100-105`" with the fork of section 6.
    64	- The note to row 97 stands as written.
    65	- Home 3 for `pick[\X\]` beside `pick` stands, with the reason of section 3 item 4 replacing the worker's.

    68	
    69	## 6. What reaches Pavol
    70	
    71	**The fork.** The compiled checker's `checkP` is the 2011–2012 team's multiple instantiation exclusion. The specification refuses it (`types-vals-vars.tex:184-189`; `trait-parameters.tex:359-367`, `:383-397`) and the library route needs it gone (61 of the 93 errors, `CLIMB-BATCH-3.md:73`). The question is which rule replaces the reliance.
    72	
    73	**The candidates and their costs.**
    74	
    75	(a) **The specification's sentence** (`overloading.tex:100-108`): overloads of a name share their static parameters; a call site instantiates them once. This is triage decision (b). Closes the hole; makes the run-time choice of instantiation moot on the checker's side. Cost: refuses the corpus sites of section 3 item 2 — `compiler_tests/Compiled12.invariantInference.fss:52-61`, `Compiled6.ak.fss:14-15`, `Library/Generator2.fss:52-57`, four interpreter tests — none of which has the hole; the triage's 35 library sites, already errors today, then need renames rather than a checker accommodation; and the reading of "static parameters" for functional methods of generic traits must be fixed (`triage.md:57-59`), or the sentence refuses overrides. Deleting or rewriting gated tests is itself a reserved stop (`PLAN.md:52`), so this choice carries that cost explicitly.

    77	(b) **The hole's exact shape, as a sub-rule of the sentence**: refuse a pair where one declaration has static parameters the other lacks and the generic one's return type depends on such a parameter, unless the more specific declaration's return type is a subtype with the parameter held rigid. Closes the hole; refuses nothing the specification permits; accepts every corpus site above; leaves decision (b) untouched. Cost: sound only if the code generator dispatches generic overloads at the call site's instantiation, which must be measured first (a generic-beside-generic pair with different bounds on a multiply-instantiated object, static type one instantiation; if the narrower-bounded declaration is chosen at the other instantiation, the rule must widen to the rigid check for generic-beside-generic pairs too, and then it is against the specification in that corner). One edit in `OverloadingOracle.satisfiesReturnTypeRule`.

    79	(c) **The interpreter's rule** (`OverloadedFunction.java:496-498`): the library was written under it and passes it. Cost: against the specification for same-parameter generic overloads with unrelated overlapping domains; which compiled tests it refuses is unmeasured.
    80	
    81	(d) **Keep the rule.** Not recommended: against the specification and the library route (section 3 item 1).
    82	
    83	**Recommendation.** (b) as the closure that lands with the relaxation, in one rung, preceded by the code-generator measurement it depends on; decision (b) of the triage — the full sentence — stays his, taken on the library evidence, and subsumes (b) here if he takes it. # Multiple instantiation exclusion: the ground for the decision

Gathered 2026-09-22 for Pavol's decision after rung P of climb batch 3 stopped: does the compiled path keep the designers' rule that no type may extend two instantiations of one generic? Nothing here decides. Sources are the rung's stop report and judge's ruling on `origin/wip/rung-exclusion-relax` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/REPORT.md`, `JUDGE.md`), the papers, the checker, the interpreter, the specification, and seven interpreter probes in `mie-probes/` (each `X.fss` with its capture `X.walk.txt`).

Terms. **Multiple instantiation inheritance**: a type extends two instantiations of one generic, for example `object Both extends { Tag[\String\], Tag[\ZZ32\] }`. **Multiple instantiation exclusion**: the rule that forbids this. **A specialised generic overload**: a generic declaration with a non-generic one beside it for one instantiation, `pick[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `pick(t: Tag[\ZZ32\])`. **Return type rule**: when a more specific overload can be chosen at run time, its return type must fit the less specific one's.

## 1. The rule in the designers' words

- The OOPSLA 2011 paper, `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`: "Fortress imposes a rule that forbids *multiple instantiation inheritance*, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor. ... We call this rule *multiple instantiation exclusion* and adopt it here." A footnote limits it to invariant parameters (`:145-150`). The stated cost is `:154-156`: "easy to enforce statically, and experience suggests that it is not onerous in practice: it is already required in Java".
- The problem it solves, from Karl Naden's writeup of 2012-08-31 (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`). The overloads `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\]): List[\X\]` and `tail(x: List[\ZZ\]): List[\ZZ\]` (`:76-81`) are unsound if some `BadList` extends both `List[\String\]` and `List[\ZZ\]`: "at runtime the more specific function for List[ZZ] would be chosen and return a List[ZZ] which is not a subtype of List[String] thus breaking type safety" (`:94-98`). Under the rule such a type "is equivalent to Bottom" (`:344-347`). With the rule in place, the return type rule may trust one instantiation: the rule "rules out any instantiation other than the one known at compile time ... We can therefore trust the instantiation known at compile time" (`:457-460`).
- What it costs: "we cannot define hasStringAndInt <: { Has[String], Has[ZZ] }" (`:470-472`). The trade-off is "specialization of generic functions or multiple instantiation inheritance, but not both" (`:477-478`). The outcome: "Ultimately, Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`:496-497`).
- The alternatives Naden discusses:
  - Filtering at run time by the expected return type, or splitting overload sets per call site (`:241-281`). He rejects both because "programmers can no longer understand the execution of a program without static type information" (`:288-290`).
  - Per-trait syntax: "allow some generic traits to be multiple instantiation excluded and others not" (`:475-477`).
  - A covariant relaxation that needs a minimal instantiation (`:536-537`).
  - The numeric tower, `:568-632`: "This restriction is problematic for expressing certain types of relationships such as the numeric hierarchy" (`:570-571`). He suggests the self type as a bound, `add[\X <: Ring[X]\](X,X): X` (`:618-624`), and ends: "more work needs to be done in order to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system" (`:631-632`). The designers left the conflict with the tower open.

## 2. The compiled checker enforces the rule and relies on it

- `checkP` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-456`): two trait types exclude when any pair of their ancestors has the same constructor with type arguments that are not equivalent (`pEqv`, `:450`). It is one of four clauses joined at `:457`. It cannot simply be deleted: with `negate` set, the same clause gives the equality constraints that static-argument inference uses (`explorations/perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md:214-217`).
- Two hierarchy checks enforce it: `scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:178` ("Types … exclude each other. … must not extend them") and `:187` ("Type … excludes … but it extends …"). `ProbeMIEPick` gets four such errors (the rung's `probes/probe-matrix.txt:22-31`).
- The return type rule relies on it. `scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105` (under `overloading/`, not `typechecker/`) solves for one instantiation of the less specific declaration (`subEDsolution`, `:88`), substitutes it into that declaration's return type (`:93-95`), and checks only that one arrow (`:97`). Relaxing `checkP` alone lets `ProbeMIEPick` link, and it then dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError: Class ProbeMIEPick$IntTag does not implement the requested interface` (`probe-matrix.txt:64-67`, and the same under every placement).

## 3. The interpreter: accepts the type, picks one instantiation, refuses the specialised overload (measured)

- Its exclusion (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/types/FType.java:197-297`) has no instantiation clause. The last test compares the leaves of `comprises` clauses (`:281-297`).
- Its overload check marks a generic parameter pair that neither subtype relation orders (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:451-455`). It refuses that pair unless some parameter pair excludes (`:495-500`, "non-ground types need exclusion"), with the message "with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (`:527`).
- Probes. All ran under `bin/fortress walk` on `main` `cfdc67f73`, JDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, with a fresh `FORTRESS_CACHES` that the first run filled:
  - `MieDecl`: the declaration is accepted. `Both` binds to a `Tag[\String\]` variable and to a `Tag[\ZZ32\]` variable, and `typecase` says it is each (`MieDecl.walk.txt:2-4`).
  - `MieInfer` has one generic function and no overloading. The interpreter infers `X` from the run-time value and takes the instantiation `Both` lists first, whatever the variable's type: `which(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` gives `Marker[\String\]` (`MieInfer.walk.txt:5`). Written explicitly, `which[\ZZ32\](Both)` gives `Marker[\ZZ32\]` (`:7`). `MieInferSwap` reverses the extends order, and the answer flips to `ZZ32` (`MieInferSwap.walk.txt:2-3`). The mechanism is `FType.java:568-574`, "We want to unify with the most specific subtype possible": the first supertype that unifies wins.
  - `MieInferRet` has no overloading either. `rz: Tag[\ZZ32\] = mk(z)` dies at run time: "RHS expression type Mk[\String\] is not assignable to LHS type Tag[\ZZ32\]" (`MieInferRet.walk.txt:3-4`).
  - `MieHeadOrId` is Naden's `headOrID` shape (`justificationOfRTR.tex:483-494`): a catch-all `headOrId(x: Any)` beside `headOrId[\X\](x: Tag[\X\]): Tag[\X\]`. The overload check accepts it, and it dies the same way (`MieHeadOrId.walk.txt:4-5`).
  - `ProbeMIEPick`, the rung's program copied unchanged, is refused at load with the `:527` message (`ProbeMIEPick.walk.txt:2-6`). It never reaches dispatch.
  - `MieTower` runs on the library's own tower. A `ZZ32` value gives `ZZ32` for `Integral`, `StandardTotalOrder` and `Equality`, and a `ZZ64` value gives `ZZ64` (`MieTower.walk.txt:2-3`). The value's own level wins.
- Answer: the interpreter accepts the declaration and picks one instantiation, the first listed. A wrong pick shows up only as a type error at the next typed binding. The interpreter refuses the specialised overload.

## 4. The specification

- Exclusion is the smallest relation: "the relations are the smallest ones that satisfy all the properties given in those sections (and this one)" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:187-189`). None of the listed properties makes two instantiations exclude (`:163-164`, `:212-216`, `:222-224`). So the type is allowed.
- "Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-340`). Its example is covariant (`:349-351`), which Naden's refinement also allows. The invariant cases are `:365-367`, "trait C is a subtrait of *every* instantiation of parametric trait D. Thus, trait C has all of the methods of every instantiation of D", and `:383-397`, `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`. `Empty` is `BadList` written on purpose (JUDGE.md §1).

# The dispatcher taking the call site's static arguments: sized in a shadow

**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. The compiler prelude is byte-identical. The 43 compiler tests that declare generic overloads all print the same. Of the 34 that link, 31 have byte-identical classes and 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`). Enforced, the specification's overload sentence refuses 179 declaration pairs in the library's apis under the narrower reading, 11 of them already errors today, and 6 gated compiler tests; a text scan finds 6 gated interpreter tests (§5).

## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today

- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
- A non-generic dispatcher with generic arms stays on the value path unless `skip` is used. The sentence makes it impossible.
- Once the sentence holds and methods are converted, the value-inference block (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`) and `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass` (`:160-213`) are dead code.

## 4. The two side defects

**A generic reached through a less specific declaration throws when its return type mentions the parameter.** The value-reading arm ends with a cast to the arm's declared return type, spelled with the arm's own parameter names (`OverloadSet.java:1720-1727`). In a dispatcher that is not a template, nothing rewrites `X`, so the cast is to the template class `Marker⟦X⟧` itself. `MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a1)` throws this way under stock and `callsite` alike (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:31-32`, `:75-76`). The same cast also goes wrong inside a template whenever the arm names its parameters differently from the dispatcher: the loader rewrites only the dispatcher's names. Stock `ScopeArms` casts to an unrewritten `Marker⟦Y⟧` (`ScopeArms.compiled.txt:5-6`). Stock `ScopeAlpha2` gets its `Marker⟦B,A⟧` rewritten with the dispatcher's map to `Marker⟦Blue,Red⟧` (`ScopeAlpha2.compiled.txt:5`). No multiple instantiation is involved in either. **The change fixes it inside templates**: a renamed arm takes the no-inference path, whose call returns the right type without that cast, and both probes pass. It leaves the defect in non-template dispatchers (`MieDispatchAny` under `callsite`) and in dotted methods. `skip` removes that path, and the sentence makes it unreachable for top-level functions, because a set that mixes generic and non-generic declarations is refused.

**A `ZZ32` instantiation made at run time is spelled differently from the static one.** `loadClosureClass` spells each argument with `RTTI.className()`, the RTTI's own Java class: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` becomes `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32` (`RTHelpers.java:174-175`, `RTTI.java:53-58`). Static code spells `ZZ32` as `com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32` (`javap-excerpts.txt:6`). The dispatcher's value path is its only caller (`OverloadSet.java:1696`). `ScopeZZ32Sub` reaches it through a template with no multiple instantiation. Stock throws: `IntSub` is not a `Sub⟦fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`ScopeZZ32Sub.compiled.txt:5`). Under `callsite` the arm is named `grab⟦X⟧` inside the template, the loader writes the call site's own spelling, and it prints `SubM[ZZ32]` (`:10`). **The change avoids the defect on the template path and does not remove it.** `MieDispatchZZ32` and `MieDispatch`'s `grab(a)` still throw under `callsite` (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:81-82`, `:58-59`), and `skip` removes that path. The two spellings remain: the generated RTTI factories also build class names from `RTTI.className()` (`RTHelpers.getRTTIclass`, `:18-54`, called from `InstantiatingClassloader.java:2810`), untouched and unmeasured here.

## 5. What the specification's overload sentence refuses, measured

**The check.** It is in `checkOverloading`'s pair loop (`OverloadingChecker.scala:383`, before the existing rules; `scope-shadow.patch`, second file, 19 code lines). Two declarations of one name are refused when their static parameters differ in number, in kind, or in bounds after positional renaming. "Static parameters" has two readings for a functional method. Under `own` it is only the method's own list. Under `lifted` the trait's parameters come first, which is how the checker already builds its arrows for a top-level set (`STypesUtil.scala:123-127`). Like every rule of this checker, the check never sees a symbolic operator (`OverloadingChecker.scala:546-550`), and in a component it sees only declarations with a body (`:117-121`). The text scan `sentence-scan.py` counts both apart. On the two library apis it agrees with the checker exactly under `own` (179 of 179, none extra) and finds 326 of 335 under `lifted`.

**The interpreter's library.** `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `RangeInternals.fsi` were checked through the zero probe's stack (`scope/sentence-library.txt`). The stack needed three adjustments for the current tree. Its memo hunks are dropped, since the tree has had its own memo since `d28cf74d0`. Its five api edits give way to the tree's own repair of the same defects (`a7ced6764`). `QQ`'s `comprises { AnyIntegral, ... }` is written as the zero stack had it, because the tree's form stops the api's check with an earlier error. The stock run gives 203 errors, the triage's figure (`sentence-library.txt:4`).

| reading | pairs refused | of them the stock rules already refuse | whole-unit errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own` | 179 | 11 | 382 |
| `lifted` | 335 | 43 | 538 |

- The 43 are the triage's 35 plus the 8 it said the sentence also reaches (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md:52-59`). The other pairs are ones the stock rules accept.

### Route A: keep the rule, flatten the tower

The tripwire test `XXXExclusionRelaxRungP` is deleted in the same change (`REPORT.md`, "The three homes").

- Interpreter: coercion called at dispatch and at typed bindings, 150-200 lines in six files, the compiled side's own mechanism (remedy i); or, without it, 160 library and 207 test sites converted by hand and the same in every future program (remedy ii). One line, `FortressLibrary.fss:4121`, is reached by every passing test, so the interpreter rung lands first (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3, § 6`).
- The compiled side's precedent for remedy (i): of the 40 programs in `library_tests/`, 12 name a type wider than `ZZ32` and 9 bind an integer literal to one, every one through the prelude's `coerce`, none by hand (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3`).

# Where a dispatched generic gets its instantiation, and route C's overload half

## 1. The instantiation: at the call site when nothing can be dispatched, from the run-time value when it can

Every probe with a multiply instantiating object links only under `-Dprobe.rungP=hier`; under `off` each such object gets the four hierarchy errors (`MieDispatch.compiled.txt:1-11`). `Both` extends `Tag[\String\]` and `Tag[\ZZ32\]` (`MieDispatch.fss:14`). Each function is `f[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\]`, so `X` is in the return type.

| call | how the call reaches the generic | prints or throws |
|---|---|---|
| `which(z)`, `z: Tag[\ZZ32\] = Both` / `which(s)`, `s: Tag[\String\]` | one declaration, no overloading | `Marker[ZZ32]` / `Marker[String]` (`MieDispatch.compiled.txt:15-16`) |
| `pick(z)` / `pick(s)` | beside `pick(p: Plain)`, whose domain excludes `Tag` | `Marker[ZZ32]` / `Marker[String]` (`:17-18`) |
| `grab(z)` / `grab(s)`, and `gz: Marker[\ZZ32\] = grab(z)`, `gs: Marker[\String\] = grab(s)` | beside the less specific `grab(a: Any): Any` | `Marker[ZZ32]` / `Marker[String]`, and each binding holds that (`:21-24`) |
| `grab(a)`, `a: Any = Both` | only by dispatch from `grab(Any)` | `ClassCastException`: `Both` cannot be cast to `Tag⟦CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`:25-27`) |
| `grab(b)`, `b: Tag[\Blue\] = Mixed`, where `Mixed extends { Sub[\Red\], Tag[\Blue\] }` and a second generic `grab[\X\](t: Sub[\X\])` is declared | the checker picks the `Tag` generic at `X = Blue`, and the `Sub` one may apply at run time | `ClassCastException`: `Marker⟦Red⟧` cannot be cast to `Marker⟦Blue⟧` (`MieDispatchSub.compiled.txt:15-18`) |

**At the call site the static argument is a constant in the name of the class the call loads.** For `grab(z)` and `grab(s)`, `run()` does `getstatic` on the closure class of `grab⟦ZZ32⟧` and `grab⟦String⟧` (`javap-excerpts.txt:12-13`):

    204: getstatic #204 // Field "MieDispatch?$\\=grab?com\\|sun\\|fortress\\|compiler\\|runtimeValues\\|FZZ32??$\\=?Arrow?MieDispatch\\%Tag?X?,…
    234: getstatic #214 // Field "MieDispatch?$\\=grab?fortress\\|CompilerBuiltin\\%String??$\\=?Arrow?MieDispatch\\%Tag?X?,…

javap prints the non-ASCII brackets as `?`, so `grab?…FZZ32??` is `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`. The code generator puts the checker's static arguments into that name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`). The class loader expands the template under that name when the class is first loaded, rewriting each method with `MethodInstantiater` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:166`). The call does not go through a dispatcher when no more specific declaration can apply at run time. Even `grab`, which has a less specific sibling, is called this way.

**When the call is dispatched, each generic arm takes its static argument from the run-time value.** The dispatcher asks the argument for its run-time type (`getRTTI`). It then asks that type for its `Tag` parameter (`Tag__1()`) and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass` (`javap-excerpts.txt:18-47`). That call builds the class name from the run-time type's own name (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:172-178`), and the loader expands the template at load. `OverloadSet.java:1411-1696` emits this for every generic arm that has type variables, the last arm included, although the comment at `:1378-1381` says the checker provides the last arm's static arguments. `:1487` says "a valid instantiation must use the runtime type".

The run-time type of `Both` records one `Tag` parameter, `ZZ32`, the one listed last (`javap-excerpts.txt:50`). The reason is that the direct supertypes are kept in a map keyed by the generic's name (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1276`). With user types the choice is visible: `RedBlue` gives `Marker[Blue]` and `BlueRed` gives `Marker[Red]` (`MieDispatchAny.compiled.txt:23-25`).

**`MieDispatchSub` shows that a call-site constant does not survive dispatch.** `grab(b)` loads `grab⟦Blue⟧` (`javap-excerpts.txt:57`). The template behind it is the dispatcher for the two generics. Its `Sub` arm reads `Red` from `Mixed`'s run-time type (`Sub__1()`, `:67-69`) and returns `Marker⟦Red⟧`. The instance's own cast to `Marker⟦X⟧`, now `Marker⟦Blue⟧` (`:71`), throws. Under the specification the set's static parameters are fixed once at the call site (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:106-108`, `trait-parameters.tex:374`). `X = Blue` would leave `Sub[\Blue\]` inapplicable, and the call would return `Marker[Blue]`. The two declarations have the same static parameters, so route B(a) (`overloading.tex:100-105`) accepts this set. Route B(b), which targets only a non-generic specialisation, accepts it too.

**B(b)'s precondition does not hold:** the code generator instantiates a dispatched generic arm from the run-time value, not from the call site, so B(b) leaves `MieDispatchSub` type-checking and failing at run time. The same holds under B(a).

Two defects found on the way do not involve multiple instantiation:
- Through a less specific declaration, a generic whose return type mentions `X` always throws. The dispatcher casts the result to the uninstantiated `Marker⟦X⟧` (`javap-excerpts.txt:46`); with `RedTag`, which is a `Tag` at one instantiation only, the result is a `ClassCastException` (`MieDispatchAny.compiled.txt:27-28`).
- An instantiation at `ZZ32` made at run time names `ZZ32` `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32`, the run-time type's class name. Static code names it `com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32`, so the instance and the object disagree. `IntTag` fails this way with no multiple instantiation (`MieDispatchZZ32.compiled.txt:4-5`), and `grab(a)` on `Both` hits this defect first.

(* No non-generic specialisation, so route B(b) would accept the overload set: the

component ScopeArms
export Executable

(* MieDispatchSub with arms that can be told apart: the Tag generic returns a TagM, the
   Sub generic a SubM, both Markers.  The Sub generic names its parameter Y, so the
   dispatcher must rename it to the Tag generic's X.  Through b: Tag[Blue] the call is
   checked as the Tag generic at X = Blue and dispatched; the specification's answer is
   TagM[Blue] for Mixed (Sub[Blue] does not apply), SubM[Blue] for SubBlue, TagM[Blue] for
   TagBlue.  Mixed needs the relaxed checkP to link. *)
trait Tag[\X\] end
trait Sub[\X\] extends Tag[\X\] end
object Red end
object Blue end
object Mixed extends { Sub[\Red\], Tag[\Blue\] } end
object SubBlue extends Sub[\Blue\] end
object TagBlue extends Tag[\Blue\] end
trait Marker[\X\] end
object TagM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end
object SubM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end

grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = TagM[\X\]
grab[\Y\](t: Sub[\Y\]): Marker[\Y\] = SubM[\Y\]

name(m: Any): String = typecase m of
    TagM[\Red\] => "TagM[Red]"
    TagM[\Blue\] => "TagM[Blue]"
    SubM[\Red\] => "SubM[Red]"
    SubM[\Blue\] => "SubM[Blue]"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
  r: Sub[\Red\] = Mixed
  println("grab(r), r: Sub[Red] = Mixed    -> " name(grab(r)))
  b1: Tag[\Blue\] = Mixed
  println("grab(b1), b1: Tag[Blue] = Mixed   -> " name(grab(b1)))
  b2: Tag[\Blue\] = SubBlue
  println("grab(b2), b2: Tag[Blue] = SubBlue -> " name(grab(b2)))
  b3: Tag[\Blue\] = TagBlue
  println("grab(b3), b3: Tag[Blue] = TagBlue -> " name(grab(b3)))
end
end

A trait or object declaration is satisfied by
a declaration
that has the same header,\footnote{The order of
the modifiers,
the clauses,
and the types in the
\KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes} and \KWD{comprises} clauses
may differ.}
and contains,
for each field declaration and non-abstract method declaration
in the exported declaration,
a satisfying declaration (or a set of declarations).
When a trait has an abstract method declared,
a satisfying trait declaration is allowed to provide a concrete declaration.
If a trait declaration (in an API)
has a \KWD{comprises} clause containing ``\EXP{\ldots}'',
then the \KWD{comprises} clause of its satisfying declaration
must contain all the types listed in the declaration in the API
but it cannot contain ``\EXP{\ldots}'';
instead, it may contain other types declared in the component
provided that those types are not declared by the API.
A field declaration is satisfied by
a (possibly implicit) getter and/or setter declaration,
depending on whether the field
is declared to be \KWD{hidden} and/or \KWD{settable}

trait Number extends { AnyAdditiveGroup, AnyMultiplicativeRing }
        comprises { RR64, QQ, AnyIntegral }
    asFloat(self): RR64
    (** Two exact numbers of different types compare as rationals; a float
        compares with any number after %asFloat%, so an exact value equals
        its nearest float. **)
    opr =(self, other:Number):Boolean =
        typecase self of
            RR64 => (asFloat(self) = asFloat(other))
            else => typecase other of
                        RR64 => (asFloat(self) = asFloat(other))
                        else => (exactValue(self) = exactValue(other))
                    end
        end
end

exactValue(x: Number): QQ =
    typecase x of
        q: QQ => q
        z: ZZ32 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: ZZ64 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: NN32 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: NN64 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: ZZ => do q: QQ = z; q end
        else => Ratio(0, 0)
    end
